title: Internal FAQ: Dedicated Throughput SLO + Tiers (Support/CS/Sales)
content:
Audience: Support, Customer Success, Sales (incl. Solutions Eng)
Owner: Product Ops (DRI: Talia) w/ Product Dedicated (Lauren)

Last updated: 2025-03-05

---

1) What changed? (1-minute summary)

We now have formal Dedicated throughput tiers (Standard / Performance / Premium) with:
- A consistent definition of “throughput” (what we measure, how we measure it)
- Clear customer-facing expectations: sustained throughput objective + burst policy + overload behavior
- Dashboards/exports for customers + internal alerting
- A shared “is this an SLO breach?” decision tree so Support/CS/Sales are aligned with SRE + Runtime

If a customer says “throughput is low,” we need to first distinguish between:
A) The system enforcing tier limits (expected throttling / admission control), vs
B) A platform-side shortfall (SLO at risk / actual breach), vs
C) A workload change that invalidates the customer’s assumptions (prompt distribution, model swap, streaming pattern, concurrency)

---

2) Key definitions (use these words consistently)

Q: What does Redwood mean by “throughput” for Dedicated?
A: Throughput is measured as effective OUTPUT token rate for successful, served traffic on a Dedicated deployment, aggregated over a rolling window.
- Think: “How many output tokens per second did the deployment actually deliver?”
- This is not the same as requests/sec.

Q: Why output tokens/sec (instead of requests/sec)?
A: Requests vary heavily by output length. Tokens/sec is the most stable and comparable measure across real workloads. Requests/sec can be derived, but it depends on avg output tokens/request.

Q: What is the SLI vs SLO?
A:
- SLI (indicator): effective_output_tokens_per_sec (deployment-level)
- SLO (objective): a minimum sustained throughput target for the tier, measured over a rolling window, with defined exclusions.

Q: What window do we use?
A: For customer-facing reporting and breach evaluation we use a rolling window (default: 5 minutes) and evaluate sustained periods, not momentary dips. (Exact window + aggregation semantics are defined in the measurement standard.)

Q: What counts as “eligible time” for the SLO?
A: Time when the deployment is available for serving and not in an excluded state.
Common exclusions:
- Planned maintenance windows (per contract)
- Customer-induced errors (e.g., invalid requests, auth failures)
- Warm-up after scale-up / node replacement (bounded; see measurement standard)
- Explicit overload mode where Redwood is enforcing admission control to protect the deployment (see below; throttling is not itself a breach)

Q: What does “admission control / throttling” mean?
A: When traffic exceeds the tier’s sustained capacity (or violates concurrency assumptions), the system may throttle (429 / 503 with a Dedicated-specific reason code) rather than letting latency spiral or cause timeouts.
- Expected behavior: throttling is the mechanism that keeps throughput predictable for admitted requests.
- Key point: “We got throttled” is usually a sign the customer hit their cap, not that Redwood missed the throughput guarantee.

---

3) Dedicated tiers (what we promise vs what we don’t)

Q: What are the tier names and how should we describe them?
A:
- Standard: baseline dedicated throughput with conservative burst, suitable for steady workloads.
- Performance: higher sustained throughput and more headroom; better for variable concurrency.
- Premium: highest sustained throughput, strictest shape/region constraints, and prioritized operational handling.

Q: What does each tier include (high level)?
A: All tiers include dedicated isolation + Redwood Dedicated operational tooling. Differences are in:
- Sustained throughput objective
- Burst allowances (how far/how long you can exceed sustained level before throttling)
- Supported hardware shapes/regions
- Overload behavior guarantees (how we fail: throttle vs degrade)
- Reporting/exports and support response targets (if applicable per contract)

Q: Are tier guarantees “unlimited if we pay more”?
A: No. Each tier has explicit throughput + concurrency assumptions. If customers need higher, we either:
- Upsize the shape, or
- Add nodes/capacity (multi-node pool), or
- Use an approved exception (priced + risk-reviewed)

Q: Do tiers guarantee a specific latency?
A: Not as the primary objective. Tiers include tail-latency guardrails and overload behavior, but the throughput SLO is the primary contractual performance metric for Dedicated in this project.

---

4) Measurement caveats (most common customer confusions)

Q: “We’re not hitting our tokens/sec, but our prompts got longer. Is that an SLO breach?”
A: Not necessarily.
- Longer prompts increase prefill cost and can reduce decode throughput (tokens/sec) depending on concurrency and caching.
- Our tier baselines assume a prompt length distribution and concurrency range. If the customer’s distribution shifts materially, we should treat it as a workload change requiring re-sizing or configuration adjustments.
What to do: Ask for prompt length distribution (p50/p95 input tokens), output length distribution, concurrency, and whether streaming is used.

Q: “Our requests/sec dropped but tokens/sec looks OK. Is Redwood underperforming?”
A: Possibly no. If average output tokens/request increased, requests/sec can drop while tokens/sec stays stable.
What to do: Reframe in tokens/sec and confirm output-length changes.

Q: “Streaming responses feel slower.”
A: Streaming changes perceived latency and can change batching efficiency.
- We measure throughput in tokens/sec, not “time to first token” (TTFT) as the primary SLO.
- If streaming settings changed (chunking, flush frequency), perceived responsiveness can change even if throughput is similar.
What to do: Check TTFT and decode rate panels; confirm client streaming consumption.

Q: “We got throttled; doesn’t that mean Redwood failed the guarantee?”
A: No—throttling can be expected and is often the designed protection.
- If throttling occurs while the deployment is still meeting sustained throughput for admitted traffic, that is working as intended.
- If throttling is happening below the tier’s stated sustained throughput under the assumed workload, that could indicate misconfiguration, capacity issues, or a genuine SLO risk.

Q: “We saw a throughput drop during a node replacement.”
A: Controlled maintenance / failover periods can be excluded, depending on contract terms and duration. For suspicious cases, SRE can confirm if the time window is marked as excluded/maintenance.

---

5) What IS an SLO breach vs. what is NOT (examples)

Use this section when writing to customers or deciding escalation severity.

A) Typically NOT a breach (expected / customer-actionable)
1. Customer is throttled because they exceeded tier burst/concurrency assumptions.
- Evidence: high throttle rate + queue depth growth + admitted throughput stable.
- Recommendation: reduce concurrency, smooth traffic, enable client-side retries w/ backoff, or upsell capacity/tier.

2. Customer changed model to a heavier variant or increased max_output_tokens.
- Evidence: same deployment, different model_id or generation settings.
- Recommendation: update sizing; run a benchmark/proposal.

3. Workload shift: input token lengths increased materially, or prompt distribution became bimodal.
- Evidence: input_tokens p95 grew; prefill time dominates; cache hit rate dropped.
- Recommendation: adjust prompts, caching strategy, or capacity.

4. Customer-side networking / client backpressure causing stalled streams.
- Evidence: server shows tokens emitted; client reports lag; socket buffer/backpressure.
- Recommendation: client investigation; confirm streaming consumption.

B) Could be a breach (needs SRE review)
1. Sustained throughput for admitted requests is below the tier objective during eligible time, under the documented assumptions.
- Evidence: throughput SLI below objective for multiple rolling windows; no corresponding throttling that explains it.

2. Platform-side regression (runtime deploy, kernel change, scheduler issue) affecting a subset of deployments.
- Evidence: multiple customers or canaries show correlated drop; recent change window.

3. Fleet capacity or noisy-neighbor-like contention inside a “dedicated” pool due to misprovisioning.
- Evidence: GPU utilization anomalies, frequent evictions, abnormal queue depth/latency, infra events.

4. Persistent overload mode below expected thresholds (e.g., admission control is kicking in “too early”).
- Evidence: throttle begins at concurrency/traffic that should be supported for that tier/shape.

C) Definitely a breach (page SRE)
1. Confirmed eligible-time sustained throughput below objective with no customer-induced cause, persisting > 15–30 minutes (or per alert definition), OR causing an active production incident.
2. Widespread impact across Dedicated fleet, or Premium customer impact.

---

6) Triage checklist (Support / CS)

When a customer reports “Dedicated throughput is low,” collect these before escalating:

Required (minimum):
- customer_org / account name
- deployment_id (or Dedicated cluster name)
- region
- tier (Standard/Performance/Premium)
- model_id + version (and any recent change)
- time range (with timezone)
- whether streaming is enabled
- expected throughput and where the expectation came from (contract language, proposal, verbal)

Strongly recommended:
- input token distribution (p50/p95) for the time range
- output token distribution (p50/p95)
- observed concurrency (avg/p95) and request rate
- throttling rate (% responses throttled) + error codes
- any recent traffic pattern changes (batch jobs, cron spikes)

Internal quick checks (10 min):
- Open the Dedicated throughput dashboard for the deployment:
  - throughput SLI vs objective line
  - throttle rate
  - queue depth / scheduler saturation
  - GPU utilization + memory
  - TTFT + decode tokens/sec panels
- Check for known incidents / maintenance in that window

---

7) Escalation paths (who to involve, and when)

If you suspect a breach or cannot explain the drop after triage:

Support (reactive tickets):
1. Create/Update customer ticket with triage checklist (use template from ENG-2222 once rolled out).
2. If likely breach: page Dedicated SRE on-call via #eng-sre-oncall and link dashboard + ticket.
3. If shape/capacity constraints suspected: loop in Infra Fleet (Vanessa/Irene) via #eng-infra.
4. If admission control/scheduler behavior suspected: loop in Runtime (Sofia/Noah/Omar) via #eng-runtime.

Customer Success (proactive + account mgmt):
- If customer is consistently hitting throttle limits: coordinate capacity upsell / resizing plan with Sales + Product.
- If Premium: treat as priority; ensure an owner and customer comms cadence.

Sales / Solutions (pre-contract or renewal):
- Do not promise req/sec guarantees.
- Do not promise “no throttling.” Throttling is part of predictable operation.
- If prospect requests an exception (higher guarantee than tier): follow exception process (Product + SRE + Finance/Legal review). Reference: SLA exception email thread process and PM-491 guidance.

---

8) Customer-safe language (copy/paste)

A) Explaining the guarantee
“Dedicated throughput is defined as sustained output tokens per second delivered by your deployment, measured over a rolling window under the tier’s documented workload assumptions. You’ll have access to the same throughput dashboard we use internally so we can jointly validate performance.”

B) Explaining throttling
“If your traffic exceeds the tier’s sustained capacity or burst policy, Redwood will intentionally throttle a portion of requests to keep the deployment stable and maintain predictable throughput for admitted requests. Throttling is the expected signal that you’re at or above your current capacity, and we can help you size up or adjust traffic shaping.”

C) Asking for the right data
“To quickly diagnose this, can you share the deployment ID, the time window, and whether prompt lengths or concurrency changed recently? The two biggest drivers of throughput variance are input/output token distributions and concurrency.”

D) When we believe it might be a platform issue
“Based on the metrics we’re seeing, your deployment’s admitted throughput was below the tier objective during eligible time. We’re escalating internally to our on-call team and will follow up with findings and next steps.”

---

9) FAQ (common Qs from Sales / Procurement)

Q: Is the throughput guarantee per model?
A: The contractual SLO is tier-based and measured on the deployed model configuration. In practice, the tier baselines assume a set of supported shapes and typical workload distributions; if a customer deploys a materially different model or context pattern, we may need to resize. (Do not frame this as “we guarantee X for every model.”)

Q: Can customers export the throughput metrics?
A: Yes—customer-visible dashboards and exportable metrics are part of the launch package. (Exact export method depends on console/telemetry enablement.)

Q: What remedies/credits apply?
A: Refer to the Dedicated throughput SLO contract language. Support/CS should not invent credits. If a breach is confirmed, route to CS + Legal/Sales Ops as appropriate.

Q: What about regional GPU supply constraints?
A: Premium (and some Performance shapes) may be limited by region. Do not sell a shape/region combination unless it’s in the supported catalog.

---

10) Open edges / known gotchas (internal)

- “Throughput vs quality”: customers may increase max_output_tokens or change sampling and then expect the same req/sec. Re-anchor on tokens/sec.
- “Single big tenant batch job”: Dedicated is isolated, but a single customer can still self-inflict overload. Admission control is the guardrail.
- “Burst misunderstandings”: burst is not a second, higher sustained guarantee. It’s a temporary allowance.
- “Deployment_id cardinality”: if a customer has multiple deployments under one contract, measure per deployment unless the contract explicitly aggregates.

---
